name: Oral minoxidil
lead: Oral minoxidil is minoxidil taken as a tablet. At high doses it is a prescription blood-pressure drug (Loniten, approved by the FDA in 1979); at much lower doses it is used off-label by dermatologists for hair loss, an approach often called low-dose oral minoxidil (LDOM) that emerged around 2015.[1][2] It has also become popular in looksmaxxing communities, where users discuss it for scalp hair, eyebrows, beard and lashes.[3][4]

Reviews report oral minoxidil as effective and generally well tolerated in hair loss, with androgenetic alopecia the most studied condition, but they call for larger randomised trials.[5][6] A 2024 randomised trial compared daily oral minoxidil with twice-daily topical 5 percent minoxidil in men over 24 weeks, and a 2024 trial of 65 patients compared 1 mg daily oral minoxidil with topical solution.[7][8] Common effects are excess hair growth (hypertrichosis) and fluid retention, and reviews note dose-dependent cardiovascular effects.[1][9]

Oral minoxidil is prescription-only and not FDA-approved for hair loss. Forum posts include reports of bloating and discussion of buying tablets without a prescription, which this wiki does not detail.
infobox: Prescription-only (US, UK); topical form is over-the-counter in the US[1]

paras: Upjohn synthesised minoxidil in 1963 and introduced it for high blood pressure in 1971, when hair growth was noticed as a side effect; the FDA approved oral tablets in 1979 and topical minoxidil for male pattern baldness in 1988.[1] Early haemodynamic and clinical experience with the drug as a vasodilator was published in 1975.[11]
Wikipedia reports that low-dose oral use for hair loss developed from about 2015, led by Rodney Sinclair and others, and that use rose sharply after an August 2022 New York Times article.[1]

Minoxidil is a prodrug converted by sulfotransferase enzymes in hair follicles to minoxidil sulfate, which opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels. Its effect on hair is not fully understood; proposed pathways include vasodilation, anti-inflammatory action, Wnt/beta-catenin signalling and an antiandrogen effect.[1][10]

A 2021 review found 17 studies with 634 patients using oral minoxidil as the main treatment for hair loss, mostly androgenetic alopecia, and concluded it was effective and well tolerated, while noting that larger randomised dose-comparison studies are needed.[5] A 2022 comparative review ranked oral minoxidil 5 mg per day below dutasteride and finasteride 5 mg per day and above finasteride 1 mg per day, with low-dose oral minoxidil lower.[10]

Randomised trials include a 2024 double-blind trial comparing oral and topical minoxidil in men over 24 weeks, a 2024 trial of 65 patients comparing oral and topical forms, and 2021 and 2022 trials in female pattern hair loss using low oral doses.[7][8][12][15] An expert review by hair-loss dermatologists in 2025 provides recommendations for safe use of topical and oral minoxidil.[2]
For alopecia areata, a European expert consensus describes oral minoxidil as an adjuvant therapy with limited supporting data.[13]

Hypertrichosis is the most common effect and is dose-dependent. Reviews also describe cardiovascular symptoms.[10] Wikipedia lists oral effects including low blood pressure, fluid and salt retention, oedema, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, headaches and temporary shedding, and rare serious events such as pericardial effusion, mostly at higher doses.[1]
A multicentre retrospective study of 1,404 patients treated with low-dose oral minoxidil for at least three months examined its systemic safety.[9] Minoxidil is also highly toxic to dogs and cats.[1]
On looksmax.org, users report bloating and under-eye discoloration on higher amounts and ask how to reduce bloat; replies suggest using topical forms instead.[3][4] These are anecdotes.

Forum threads discuss oral minoxidil for scalp hair, eyebrows, beard and lashes, including questions from teenagers about using it during puberty.[3][4][14] Some users advise topical minoxidil or dermastamping for the same areas and limit oral use to hair loss with low body fat.[3][4]

Controlled trials of oral minoxidil exist for androgenetic alopecia in men and women, including a 2024 double-blind trial versus topical minoxidil, trials of low oral doses in female pattern hair loss and others.[7][8][12][15] Registered studies include a phase 3 trial in female androgenetic alopecia with 520 participants and a planned phase 3 trial in men.[16][17] No trial of oral minoxidil for eyebrow, beard or eyelash growth in healthy people appears in these sources.

timeline.event: Introduced for high blood pressure; hair growth noticed as a side effect.[1]
FDA approves oral minoxidil (Loniten) for hypertension.[1]
FDA approves topical minoxidil (Rogaine) for male pattern baldness.[1]
Low-dose oral minoxidil for hair loss emerges.[1]
Use rises sharply after an August New York Times article.[1]

lore.intro: Users on looksmax.org discuss oral minoxidil as a stronger, easier alternative to topical minoxidil for hair, brows, beard and lashes, alongside concerns about bloat and sourcing.[3][4][14]

claims.claim: Oral minoxidil is a convenient alternative to topical for hair loss.
claims.believers: Users cite not having to apply a solution; some suggest topical for those who experience side effects.[3][4]
claims.experts: Reviews report it as effective and well tolerated and note topical compliance problems; trials against topical exist, with larger dose-comparison studies still needed.[1][5][7]

claims.claim: It grows eyebrows, beard and lashes.
claims.believers: Forum threads ask how much oral minoxidil would do for brows and lashes.[14]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists beard growth as an off-label topical use; no trial of oral minoxidil for brows or lashes is described in these sources.[1]

claims.claim: Oral minoxidil causes bloating and can harm the heart.
claims.believers: Users report bloat and under-eye discoloration.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists fluid retention, oedema and rare pericardial effusion; reviews describe cardiovascular effects as dose-dependent.[1][10]

claims.claim: Teenagers can take it for hair or facial hair.
claims.believers: Posters aged 15 ask how and when to start.[4]
claims.experts: The published trials described here are in adults, and no study of oral minoxidil for cosmetic use during puberty is described in these sources.[5]

card.summary: Pill minoxidil at low doses for hair loss; trial-backed and widely prescribed off-label, with fluid-retention and heart caveats.
card.note: Off-label and prescription-only; reported effects include hypertrichosis, fluid retention and rare cardiac events.

quick.overview:
Oral minoxidil is the blood-pressure pill minoxidil used at very low doses, off-label, for hair loss. Dermatologists prescribe it as an alternative to topical minoxidil, and looksmaxxing users also discuss it for brows, beard and lashes.

Reviews and several randomised trials support its use in androgenetic alopecia, though larger dose-comparison studies are still wanted. Results last only while treatment continues.
quick.mechanism: It is a prodrug converted in hair follicles to minoxidil sulfate, which opens potassium channels; proposed effects include vasodilation, anti-inflammatory action and growth-pathway signalling.
quick.risks: Common effects are excess body hair and fluid retention; others include low blood pressure, rapid heartbeat, headache and, rarely, pericardial effusion. Forum users report bloating. It is prescription-only and not approved for hair loss, and is toxic to pets.
